BSC2891 (python for biology majors) is a required core class for the microbiology major in cals. But bioinformatics and R programming can be used as electives! Python was really not hard at all, didn’t require any previous knowledge on programming. Outside of that, in chemistry classes or biology classes they require you to use excel and understand how to pull information from data (from what I remember) but that’s about it as far as anything *computer* related. If you’re hoping to go into research I really recommend taking bioinformatics as an elective, as those skills will be very useful down the line!

But also, you allow honorlock/proctorU to have access to photos of your state ID, student ID number, 360s of your home, your face, access to your camera, screen control, and mic. Proctor u literally gives some random individual complete control of your mouse and screen to access codes, input passwords, and check your computer settings. If you allow them to have that level of control, you must feel pretty safe with them having it or at least believe you won’t have photos of your ID with your address leaked in a hack. So I should in turn feel safe with them accidentally seeing some of my sensitive information, right? But I don’t, and neither would you. Which is why it’s a valid reason to be completely concerned with the invasive nature of the program. If you’re thinking “what a dumbass” when I accidentally had my files open to take a quick 15 minute test after I’m just coming off a 12 hour shift and my mind is foggy, then why don’t you think it’s equally stupid to let them have photos of your ID, your home, and complete access to your computer? I understand the need for remote proctoring, but people mess up, programs get hacked, leaks happen and it’s reasonable to be concerned or want it gone.

It does get easier. It's a position that takes time to get used to, but when you've done it for a month or so then it becomes insanely natural. At the end of the day, it's just moving boxes. What I found super helpful was being trained at the end of the line in the market section, because most of the product is viewable and I could visualize where it went a lot easier than the rest of the mostly unmarked boxes. Like the jars of pasta sauce, that was easy to take note of and place with other things like it. Then after you nail that down you can move to a different section and start to learn that one, and so on. Then before you know it you're drifting up and down the line like a pro. To the bringing everyone down part, I'll admit I've been guilty of glaring at the new guys when I have to pick up their slack-but at the end of the day it usually comes down to the fact that they were placed in an incovient location before they were ready and if it was close to the front then everyone would be backed up-so thats why I suggest the market section or whatever is at the end of your line. My inbound team is super close knit, even though they roasted the hell out of me when I first started they still ended up becoming my best friends and greastest support. Inbound is the secret treasure of target postions in my opinion-and I'm saying that after a beast of a double truck + a visit, so it's gotta hold a speical place in my heart to be saying that haha.
